title: Certificate of Compliance vs. Certificate of Conformance in Electronics Manufacturing
summary: Certificate of Compliance vs. Certificate of Conformance: what each CoC actually certifies, why the title isn’t proof, and 5 checks before you accept one.
body_markdown:
##


Welcome to one of the more irritating little ambiguities in electronic component procurement. Everyone uses the same three letters, but they can mean two different things, and to top it all off those two meanings get confused.


Whether it’s electronic components, PCBs, or assemblies, you will eventually encounter a request for a CoC, but that doesn’t tell you if the requestor wants a[Certificate of Conformance or a Certificate of Compliance](https://www.digikey.com/en/help-support/products/obtain-coc) . And to add to the confusion, there is no universal electronics-industry rule that separates the two terms.


There is, however, a useful practical distinction:


- A Certificate of Conformance generally answers: Does this product conform to the specified requirements?
- A Certificate of Compliance generally answers: Does this product comply with the applicable standard, regulation, or other compliance requirement?


That distinction gives you a good starting point. Just don't treat it as a naming law. The document's actual scope matters far more than whatever somebody typed across the top of the PDF.


## What Is a Certificate of Conformance?


A Certificate of Conformance is generally an attestation that an identified product or shipment conforms to specified requirements.


Those requirements might come from a manufacturer's technical specification, customer drawing, purchase order, part revision, workmanship requirement, manufacturing specification, or contractually required inspection or testing.


The familiar electronics version goes something like this: You order a specific part built to a defined specification. The manufacturer ships the parts and issues a Certificate of Conformance stating that the supplied product conforms to the applicable specifications.


Texas Instruments, for example, calls its order documentation a "[Certificate of Conformance (CoC)](https://www.ti.com/ordering-resources/faqs/purchasing-online/certificates-of-conformance.html) ." Arrow supplier requirements provide another useful example, with certificate information that can include the manufacturer, manufacturer part number and revision, purchase order, quantity, date code, lot code, and applicable customer drawing and revision.


[Raytheon](https://qnotes.raytheon.com/files/RQN_UK_10.pdf) has likewise used Certificate of Conformance requirements tied directly to fulfillment of purchase-order requirements.


That last point is important because it tells you what a Certificate of Conformance really is: an attestation. The certificate says the requirements were met. It is not necessarily the objective evidence demonstrating that they were met.


## What Is a Certificate of Compliance?


A Certificate of Compliance is generally an attestation that a product, material, or process complies with an identified requirement such as a regulation, standard, material restriction, or customer compliance requirement.


In electronics we encounter Certificates of Compliance associated with RoHS, REACH-related substance requirements, material restrictions, environmental requirements, or specific industry standards.


The useful question here is: *Compliance with what?*


A document that simply says "Certificate of Compliance" without identifying the requirement leaves you with an awfully large blank to fill in yourself.


You also need to distinguish a supplier compliance statement from more specialized evidence or regulatory documentation. Depending on the requirement, you may instead need a material declaration, laboratory test report, Certificate of Analysis, third-party certification, or formal Declaration of Conformity.


RoHS is a good example. Under[EU RoHS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/65/2026-07-01/eng) , manufacturers of covered electrical and electronic equipment have specific responsibilities involving technical documentation, internal production control, an EU Declaration of Conformity, and CE marking. An upstream supplier's RoHS Certificate of Compliance can be useful evidence in that process, but possessing one does not automatically satisfy the finished-product manufacturer's regulatory obligations.

## Certificate of Compliance vs. Certificate of Conformance: The Difference at a Glance


This is a practical way to understand the terminology, not a universally enforced definition. ISO/IEC conformity-assessment vocabulary does not establish an electronics-wide rule dividing "compliance" and "conformance" along these lines.[ISO/IEC 17050](https://www.iso.org/standard/29373.html) allows supplier declarations of conformity to concern specified requirements that can include standards, technical specifications, laws, and regulations.


Real electronics companies are similarly inconsistent. Texas Instruments uses Certificate of Conformance. DigiKey refers to a manufacturer's Certificate of Compliance. NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) uses Certificate of Compliance in PCB and PWA procurement documentation. Sanmina uses both terms in different supplier-quality contexts.


So the distinction is useful right up until your purchase order says otherwise.


## When the Industry Doesn't Follow the Terminology


JPL gives you a particularly good example of why reading the document beats relying on its title.


Certain JPL printed wiring board and printed wiring assembly procurement requirements call for a Certificate of Compliance. That certificate can identify the purchase order and line item, part number and revision, quantity, serial or screening lot, manufacturing location, date or lot information, and supplier authorization.


Functionally, that sounds quite a lot like the Certificate of Conformance we just described: an attestation about delivered hardware and fulfillment of procurement requirements.


Nothing is wrong with JPL's terminology. JPL defines the required documentation for its procurement system, and that definition governs the transaction.


As a buyer, you should treat "Compliance" and "Conformance" as clues about what you are likely to receive. Then read what the certificate actually certifies.


## What Does a Certificate Actually Prove?


A Certificate of Compliance or Certificate of Conformance is a statement. The evidence supporting that statement is a separate question.


Possessing a generic CoC does not, by itself, establish that every component was tested, that a sample was tested, that an independent laboratory performed testing, that incoming or final inspection occurred, that the component is authentic, or that a particular IPC standard applies.


What sits behind the certificate depends on the requirements being certified.


Underlying requirements might include inspection records, electrical test results, manufacturing travelers, production records, lot/date-code traceability, serial-number records, Certificates of Analysis, material declarations, calibration records, or documentation from sub-tier suppliers.


JPL's[end-item documentation](https://supplierportal.jpl.nasa.gov/qcprint.php?clause=QC123) requirements make the distinction especially visible. Its Certificate of Compliance can sit alongside a much larger package containing manufacturing, inspection, test, material, nonconformance, rework, X-ray, and process records.


The certificate is therefore better understood as the top sheet of the story, rather than the whole stack of evidence.


This distinction also matters when authenticity is involved. A certificate can contribute to component pedigree, but a nice PDF with a signature block cannot establish an unbroken chain of custody by itself. Source authorization, lot and date-code traceability, inspection, authentication, and transaction history may all matter depending on your sourcing risk and contractual requirements.


And yes, you read that right, Chain of Custody is yet another meaning for CoC!

## Certificates of Conformance Under FAR and DFARS


Federal contracting gives "Certificate of Conformance" a more specific meaning.


FAR 52.246-15 defines a Certificate of Conformance within a particular U.S. government contracting context. Under the clause, the contractor certifies that the supplied products or services conform in all respects with the applicable contract requirements.


When the clause is authorized, the certificate can permit shipment in circumstances where source inspection would otherwise be required. That does not wipe away the government's inspection rights. The FAR clause preserves the government's ability to inspect and reject defective supplies.


[DFARS](https://www.acquisition.gov/dfars/252.246-7008-sources-electronic-parts) builds additional controls around this environment for certain defense procurements, including electronic-parts sourcing and counterfeit-risk controls.


This is a different animal from a random commercial supplier attaching a PDF named CoC.pdf to your shipping notice.


When FAR, DFARS, a customer specification, regulation, purchase order, or contract gives a certificate a specific definition, that governing requirement controls. You should not assume that every supplier document titled Certificate of Conformance carries the meaning or legal effect of a FAR Certificate of Conformance.


## How to Review a Certificate of Compliance or Conformance


When a CoC is required, checking that a document exists is only the beginning. You want to know whether the document you received satisfies the requirement that caused you to request it.


### **1. Who issued it?**


Identify the party actually making the statement.


Was it the original component manufacturer, PCB fabricator, EMS provider, authorized distributor, or independent distributor?


That distinction can materially change the certificate's evidentiary value.[DigiKey](https://www.digikey.com/en/help-support/products/obtain-coc) , for example, explicitly describes supplying a manufacturer's Certificate of Compliance when the manufacturer has made one available. In that case, the distributor is providing access to the manufacturer's document rather than magically becoming the manufacturer.


### **2. What product does it cover?**


Match the certificate to the material in front of you.


Depending on your procurement requirements, that could mean checking the manufacturer, part number, revision, quantity, lot code, date code, and serial number.


A beautifully formatted certificate for the wrong revision is still documentation for the wrong revision.


### **3. What is being certified?**


Look for the requirement behind the statement.


Is the supplier certifying against a technical specification, drawing, purchase order, customer quality clause, RoHS requirement, material restriction, or industry standard?


Specificity is your friend here. "We certify that these products comply" is much less useful when the document never tells you what they supposedly comply with.


### **4. What evidence supports the certification?**


In some cases, you may need to move one layer down.


Was conformity established through inspection, testing, material declarations, manufacturing records, sub-tier documentation, traceability records, or some combination?


You may not need every underlying record delivered with every shipment. You should understand what evidence exists when the procurement requirement makes that evidence relevant.


This question is especially useful with your CM or EMS provider because certificate retention and retrieval are part of the larger traceability problem. A certificate that technically exists but takes three weeks and six email threads to associate with a particular build is not doing your quality team many favors.


Read More:[7 Compliance Questions for Your CM/EMS](https://www.cofactr.com/articles/what-your-cmems-should-be-able-to-answer-about-parts-compliance-and-quality)


### **5. Does it satisfy the actual procurement requirement?**


This is the final check, and probably the most important one.


Go back to the document that created the requirement: the purchase order, drawing, supplier-quality agreement, customer flow-down, contract, or applicable regulation.


Compare that requirement with what you actually received.


If the PO requires a manufacturer CoC tied to the manufacturer part number, revision, lot, and date code, a generic distributor compliance statement may not satisfy it. If your regulatory process requires a material declaration, a shipment Certificate of Conformance may not answer the question. If your customer requires test results, the presence of a CoC does not make those results optional unless the governing requirement says it does.


## Read What the CoC Certifies


The practical distinction is still worth remembering. Certificate of Conformance generally refers to whether a product meets specified requirements, while Certificate of Compliance commonly refers to whether a product meets an applicable standard, regulation, or compliance requirement.


Then electronics procurement does what electronics procurement does and supplies plenty of exceptions.


Some companies use the terms differently. Some use both. The abbreviation CoC can refer to either one. Formal environments such as[FAR contracting](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/52.246-15) can give Certificate of Conformance a specific contractual meaning that you should not transfer to ordinary commercial documentation.


Your safest purchasing habit is to stop treating "Do we have a CoC?" as the whole question.


Understand what you really need. Ask who issued it. Check which product, lot, revision, or shipment it covers. Identify exactly what requirement the issuer is certifying against. Understand what evidence supports that statement. Then compare the document with what your purchase order, customer, contract, or regulatory process actually requires.


That takes more time than just checking whether a PDF exists in the folder, but it can save you from discovering much later that the CoC you provided wasn’t the CoC requested.

## Frequently Asked Questions


**What is the difference between a Certificate of Compliance and Certificate of Conformance?**


In electronics manufacturing, both documents attest that specified requirements were met. Compliance often references regulations or standards, while conformance often references specifications, drawings, or purchase-order requirements.


**Why does the meaning of a CoC vary between electronics suppliers?**


No electronics-wide definition separates the two terms. Companies including Texas Instruments, DigiKey, JPL, and Sanmina use Compliance and Conformance differently within their procurement systems.


**How to review a Certificate of Compliance or Certificate of Conformance?**


Check the issuer, product identification, applicable requirements, supporting evidence, and procurement requirement. Match part numbers, revisions, quantities, lot codes, and date codes where required.


**Can I use a CoC as proof that electronic components were tested?**


No. A CoC alone does not establish independent testing, sample testing, 100% testing, incoming inspection, or final inspection. Those claims require supporting records or contractual requirements.


**Is it safe to use a CoC as proof that electronic components are authentic?**


A CoC can support component pedigree, but it does not prove authenticity alone. Buyers should examine authorized sourcing, manufacturer identity, chain of custody, and traceability documentation.


**What is typically included on an electronics Certificate of Conformance?**


Common fields include manufacturer, part number, purchase order, revision, quantity, lot or date code, applicable specification, and authorized signature. Exact requirements depend on the governing document.


**Who is responsible for issuing a CoC in electronics manufacturing?**


A CoC may come from a component manufacturer, PCB fabricator, EMS provider, distributor, or another supplier. The issuer and governing procurement requirements determine its evidentiary significance.


**Can I use a supplier's RoHS Certificate of Compliance for regulatory compliance?**


A supplier RoHS certificate can support technical documentation, but it does not automatically satisfy a finished-product manufacturer's regulatory obligations, including applicable conformity documentation and declarations.


**Do I need to specify CoC requirements on my purchase order?**


Clear purchase-order requirements reduce ambiguity. Specify the certificate type, issuer, covered products, traceability fields, applicable specifications, test documentation, and other evidence your quality process requires.
